paragraphs: Early word learning involves two connected sources of evidence. A child can notice that a word repeatedly occurs alongside a particular object or referent, and can use the social circumstances of an utterance to interpret it. The difficulty is that neither word meanings nor the relevance of social cues is necessarily known in advance.

The paper develops a Bayesian model that combines evidence about words and referents across situations. An extension also learns which social cues help determine what a speaker means. This makes the relevance of social information something the model can infer through learning, alongside the word associations it is trying to establish.

On a small collection of mother-infant interactions, the model performs better than competing models. It also accounts for experimental phenomena involving mutual exclusivity, fast mapping, and generalization from social cues. These findings support the framework as an account of several aspects of word learning within one probabilistic approach; the reported comparison is specifically grounded in a small interaction corpus.
neurips-2007-a-bayesian-framework-for-cr.tldr: A Bayesian model learns word meanings across situations and can also learn which social cues help identify intended referents.

paragraphs: An organism acting in a changing environment must continually estimate what is happening from uncertain sensory information. Neural networks face an additional challenge: their observations arrive as sequences of spikes. The paper asks how networks could use those events to carry out the Bayesian estimation and prediction computations attributed to perception and action.

The approach draws on mathematical results for continuous-time point-process filtering, a framework suited to observations arriving as discrete events over time. Using these results, the authors show how linear neural networks may implement optimal real-time state estimation and prediction in a general setting. This addresses restrictions associated with approximations used in earlier network implementations.

Several examples demonstrate the applicability of the construction. The analysis also connects the network properties required for these computations to the statistical properties of the environment. That connection provides a way to quantify how compatible a network is with its environment. The contribution is a mathematical implementation account, rather than evidence that cortical networks necessarily use this exact mechanism.
neurips-2007-a-neural-network-implementi.tldr: Point-process filtering provides a mathematical route for linear neural networks to estimate and predict environmental states optimally from sensory spikes.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models become difficult to train when they contain many unobserved variables and dependencies that do not break into convenient pieces. Those dependencies may be important for describing the data, yet inference in the resulting model can become computationally intractable. The paper addresses how to retain useful dependencies while keeping learning manageable.

Its central idea is to train several tractable submodels and encourage them to agree about the hidden variables. Each submodel supports manageable inference, while agreement connects the explanations they learn. The authors introduce an objective function for this approach and derive parameter-estimation algorithms in the style of expectation maximization.

The approach therefore places coordination among simpler models at the center of learning, allowing the collection to capture aspects of the data that do not decompose easily. Experiments on three challenging real-world learning tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms. The stated contribution combines a learning objective, a practical estimation procedure, and empirical support for using agreement to connect tractable models.
neurips-2007-agreement-based-learning-ee.tldr: Training tractable submodels to agree on hidden variables offers a manageable way to learn complex probabilistic dependencies.

paragraphs: Removing reverberation from speech requires identifying how a room changes the original sound. Blind channel identification attempts this without knowing the source signal, which creates ambiguities among possible explanations of the microphone recordings. The paper proposes an acoustic model intended to address these ambiguities while still representing real recording environments.

The model represents a room impulse response as a sparse finite impulse response filter, with relatively few active filter coefficients. Under this assumption, identifying a system with one source and multiple outputs becomes a least-squares problem with an l1 penalty. The resulting optimization is convex and can be solved efficiently with guaranteed global convergence.

The penalty parameters determine how strongly the solution favors sparsity. A Bayesian learning scheme infers those parameters directly from microphone observations, making their selection part of the method. Reported results show effective, robust source estimation in real acoustic environments, with high fidelity to measurements made in an anechoic chamber. The optimization guarantee applies to the formulated problem under the sparse response model.
neurips-2007-blind-channel-identificatio.tldr: A sparse room-response model turns blind acoustic channel identification into convex optimization, with Bayesian learning selecting the sparsity penalties.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to locate abrupt changes in a one-dimensional signal that stays constant between changes and is observed in white noise. The challenge is to distinguish genuine shifts in the underlying level from fluctuations introduced by noise. Its approach translates the search for change locations into a variable-selection problem.

The method uses a least-squares fitting criterion together with an l1-type penalty. In this formulation, selecting variables corresponds to identifying changes in the signal. The penalty makes selection part of the fitting objective, connecting change-point estimation to sparse regression methods rather than treating every possible change location as an independent decision.

The authors prove consistency of the estimated change points within an appropriate asymptotic framework. This is a qualified large-sample result, rather than a claim of exact recovery for every noisy signal. For practical implementation, they combine the LAR algorithm with a reduced dynamic-programming procedure and apply the method to synthetic and real data. The contribution links a statistical guarantee to a concrete computational approach.
neurips-2007-catching-change-points-with.tldr: Recasting change-point detection as sparse variable selection yields an l1-penalized method with consistency guarantees in an appropriate asymptotic setting.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering can be framed around the order in which items should be presented to a user. In that setting, the central output is a ranking: which items should appear ahead of others. The paper adopts this perspective and makes ranking quality the explicit target of learning.

The proposed method uses maximum-margin matrix factorization together with structured output prediction. Matrix factorization supplies the collaborative model, while structured prediction allows the learning objective to operate on rankings. This matters because a ranking describes relationships among multiple items, and the authors optimize ranking scores directly instead of using rating prediction as the training target.

The experiments report very good ranking scores and favorable scaling on collaborative-filtering tasks. These findings support the practicality of aligning the optimization objective with the ordered recommendations the method is meant to produce. The paper's stated contribution is therefore both methodological and empirical: it connects a factorization approach to direct ranking optimization and demonstrates useful performance and scalability in the tested tasks.
neurips-2007-cofi-rank-maximum-margin-ma.tldr: COFI RANK combines maximum-margin matrix factorization with structured prediction to optimize recommendation rankings directly.

paragraphs: Topic models require inference procedures that recover hidden structure from observations. Variational methods offer useful properties for this task, including convenient convergence assessment, optimization without maintaining detailed balance, and a bound on marginal likelihood. The paper builds on collapsed variational inference, which had provided an accurate approach for latent Dirichlet allocation.

The existing technique did not address model selection or inference for hyperparameters. The authors generalize it to handle both issues, producing a variational algorithm for hierarchical Dirichlet processes and for the hyperparameters of Dirichlet variables. This broadens the method beyond inference within the earlier LDA formulation and incorporates additional parts of the modeling problem.

The authors present their method as the first variational algorithm to cover these capabilities, and experiments show a significant improvement in accuracy. The result matters because the computational attractions of variational inference are retained while expanding what the procedure can infer. The reported accuracy improvement supplies empirical support for that extension, alongside its contribution to inference methodology for topic models.
neurips-2007-collapsed-variational-infer.tldr: Generalizing collapsed variational inference enables hierarchical Dirichlet process modeling and hyperparameter inference, with improved accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper connects two ways of understanding equilibrium in games. One defines stability through a specified collection of changes a player could make to their strategy. The other asks what happens when players repeatedly choose actions using learning algorithms that protect their long-run payoffs against those changes.

Such no-regret algorithms ensure that a player's accumulated performance approaches what they could have achieved by consistently applying an allowed deviation. The authors prove a computational equivalence: for a given deviation family, efficient approximation of the relevant fixed points is possible if and only if efficient no-regret algorithms resistant to those deviations exist.

They also show that when all players use no-regret algorithms, the empirical distribution of their play converges to an equilibrium. The object converging is the distribution formed from repeated actions, which is important for interpreting the result. Together, the findings connect the computational task of constructing learning rules to fixed-point approximation and explain how repeated, payoff-conscious behavior produces equilibrium at the distributional level.
neurips-2007-computational-equivalence-o.tldr: Efficient fixed-point approximation and efficient no-regret learning are computationally equivalent for the specified deviations, linking repeated play to equilibrium.

paragraphs: Density estimation describes how observations are distributed. This paper proposes a semiparametric approach that combines parametric and nonparametric criteria by changing the assumptions made about the observations. Samples remain independent, but their distributions can be encouraged to resemble one another without requiring them all to be identical.

A single scalar parameter controls this resemblance through a Bhattacharyya affinity penalty between pairs of sample distributions. Adjusting it smoothly connects the independent-sampling extreme with the independent-and-identically-distributed extreme. This provides a way to represent nonstationarity, where the data distribution varies, without introducing the strong hidden-variable assumptions associated with alternative modeling approaches discussed by the authors.

The resulting independently similarly distributed method retains certain consistency and unimodality properties resembling those of maximum-likelihood estimation. These are specific properties of the proposed scheme, rather than a blanket guarantee for every estimation problem. Experiments across several datasets support its value relative to independent, identically distributed, and mixture-modeling approaches. The central contribution is a tunable sampling assumption that couples distributional flexibility with useful estimation properties.
neurips-2007-density-estimation-under-in.tldr: A tunable similarity penalty between sample distributions connects independent and identically distributed density estimation while accommodating nonstationarity.

paragraphs: Rankings and data-association problems often involve uncertainty over permutations. With n items there are n! possible arrangements, and valid arrangements must obey mutual-exclusion constraints. These constraints make it difficult to represent the uncertainty compactly using standard graphical models, even before attempting to update that representation with new information.

The paper represents distributions using low-frequency components of a Fourier decomposition. It introduces Kronecker conditioning, an efficient procedure for maintaining these representations directly in the Fourier domain. The approach therefore combines a compact approximation with an inference operation that works within the same mathematical representation.

Truncating the Fourier representation can produce a function that is not a valid probability distribution. To address this, the authors formulate an efficient quadratic program that projects the approximation onto a relaxed marginal polytope, a relaxed set of consistency constraints. The relaxation is part of the proposed remedy. A camera-based task involving tracking multiple people demonstrates the approach's effectiveness in a real setting where competing identity assignments must be represented.
neurips-2007-efficient-inference-for-dis.tldr: Fourier approximations and Kronecker conditioning enable compact inference over permutations, with a quadratic-programming correction for relaxed probability consistency.

paragraphs: The paper explores how modeled visual neurons can distinguish motion velocities. It transfers two ideas from disparity-energy models—position tuning and phase-shift tuning—to motion-energy neurons. The aim is to construct detectors whose response properties provide a useful intermediate form of motion tuning.

The authors identify Reichardt-like detectors as examples of position tuning. They identify motion-energy filters with complex receptive fields that separate into spatial and temporal components as examples of phase tuning. Combining the two detector types creates an architecture whose center frequencies can be adjusted through both position shifts and phase shifts.

The resulting neurons have tuning between purely space-time-separable responses and pure speed tuning, resembling properties reported for neurons in primary visual cortex. The paper proposes a functional role for this intermediate tuning: comparisons between pairs of the modeled neurons can reliably distinguish velocities above or below a reference velocity. This demonstration supports the usefulness of the architecture for velocity discrimination without establishing that biological neurons necessarily perform the proposed comparison.
neurips-2007-extending-position-phase-sh.tldr: Combining position and phase tuning produces motion-energy neurons whose paired responses can distinguish velocities above or below a reference.

paragraphs: Rosetta searches for protein structures through Monte Carlo energy minimization, using many random restarts to find low-energy candidates. This paper asks whether information from an initial search can make a later search more productive. The proposed resampling method targets small proteins containing both alpha and beta structural elements.

After an initial round of Rosetta sampling, the method learns which structural features are associated with low energy. It uses two feature-selection approaches: l1-regularized linear regression and decision trees. Rather than fitting the entire energy landscape, it extracts selected structural properties and enriches those properties in a second sampling round.

This creates a feedback loop in which the first search helps guide the next search toward lower-energy structures. Across a benchmark of nine small alpha/beta proteins, the methods seldom impair Rosetta's performance and frequently improve it. The result supports selective reuse of information from earlier samples, while retaining the reported qualification that improvement is frequent rather than universal and is demonstrated on the specified benchmark.
neurips-2007-feature-selection-methods-f.tldr: Learning useful structural features from an initial Rosetta run helps guide resampling and frequently improves performance on nine small alpha/beta proteins.

paragraphs: The paper studies batch reinforcement learning when both states and actions are continuous. The learner must construct a good policy from a trajectory previously generated by another policy. A stated requirement is that this trajectory be sufficiently rich, so the learning problem depends on the information already available in the collected experience.

The authors modify fitted Q-iteration, a value-function-based learning approach. They replace greedy action selection with a search over a restricted collection of candidate policies. The search selects a policy by maximizing average action values, shifting the improvement step toward choosing among whole candidate policies using the estimated values.

The main contribution is a rigorous theoretical analysis of this variant, including finite-time bounds. Such bounds characterize the algorithm's behavior after a finite amount of learning rather than describing only an eventual limit. The authors believe these are the first bounds of this kind for value-function methods with continuous states and actions. The result concerns the analyzed algorithm and its setting, including the restricted policy collection and sufficiently rich trajectory.
neurips-2007-fitted-q-iteration-in-conti.tldr: A fitted Q-iteration variant searches a restricted policy class and receives finite-time theoretical bounds for continuous-state, continuous-action batch learning.

paragraphs: Statistical models often use explanatory variables that have a meaningful hierarchical organization. The paper introduces a general way to incorporate that organization into model fitting. Prior information enters through a penalty, allowing the relationship among variables to influence which parts of the model receive substantial weight.

The proposed penalty is convex and operates at two connected levels. It performs soft selection among groups while shrinking the variables within each group. This favors solutions with only a few leading terms in the final combination, making the hierarchy relevant both to group importance and to the contributions of individual variables.

The authors show the framework's usefulness in linear regression when several parameters together describe the influence of one feature. They also apply it to kernel regression for learning multiple kernels. These applications illustrate why grouping matters: the meaningful unit of explanation can span several parameters. Hierarchical penalization provides a common fitting framework for using that structure, while its convex formulation connects the statistical objective to a tractable class of optimization problems.
neurips-2007-hierarchical-penalization-c.tldr: A convex hierarchical penalty uses prior variable groupings to softly select groups and shrink their members in regression models.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a shared modeling framework for nonparametric Bayesian models, topic models, and Bayesian networks. Called infinite state Bayes nets, these models can represent structured domains such as words within documents or features within images. The goal is to describe several kinds of probabilistic structure within one general construction.

An infinite state Bayes net can be viewed as a directed network of hierarchical Dirichlet processes. The authors also provide an efficient way to perform collapsed Gibbs sampling in these models. Their inference procedure exploits the Bayesian network's structure and uses forward filtering followed by backward sampling on junction trees.

The framework encompasses existing models, including nested Dirichlet processes, Pachinko allocation, and mixed-membership stochastic block models, as well as new constructions. This unification matters because the same modeling language and inference strategy can serve multiple structured-data settings. Two experiments illustrate the ideas. Their stated role is illustrative, while the central methodological contribution is the general framework and the efficient sampling procedure that makes inference within it possible.
neurips-2007-infinite-state-bayes-nets-f.tldr: Infinite state Bayes nets unify several structured Bayesian model families and support efficient collapsed Gibbs sampling through network-aware inference.

paragraphs: Sparse coding learns image components so that each image can be represented with relatively few active coefficients. When trained on natural images, the learned components can resemble receptive fields in primary visual cortex. However, the resulting coefficients still show substantial statistical dependencies, conflicting with the model's assumption that they are independent.

The paper extends the prior over coefficient activity states with a pairwise coupling term. This gives the model a way to represent relationships between the activity of different image components. Learning from natural-image statistics then adjusts both the representation of activity and the interactions connecting neighboring basis functions.

The learned couplings include facilitatory and inhibitory interactions: relationships that favor or discourage joint activity. The authors suggest that these interactions may help explain the function of horizontal connections in primary visual cortex, and discuss implications for physiological experiments. The biological interpretation remains a possible explanation. The direct modeling result is that accounting for residual dependencies produces learned interactions with both supportive and suppressive effects.
neurips-2007-learning-horizontal-connect.tldr: Adding learned pairwise interactions to sparse coding captures coefficient dependencies and suggests a possible role for horizontal connections in visual cortex.

paragraphs: Visual attributes describe qualities such as color, stripes, or spots. This paper develops a probabilistic generative model that represents an attribute through recurring patterns of image segments. The shared properties can involve appearance, shape, spatial arrangement, or combinations of these features, allowing the model to express several kinds of visual regularity.

The representation also handles attributes defined by a general relationship among appearances. Stripes, for example, can involve alternating colors without requiring one particular pair of colors. Although the model is generative, its learning procedure is discriminative: it optimizes a likelihood ratio so that training can use images without supplied segmentations.

Experiments demonstrate learning across a broad range of attributes in a weakly supervised setting. The authors show a workflow beginning with a text query to Google image search and ending with a model that recognizes an attribute and identifies its spatial extent in new real-world images. The contribution connects flexible attribute representations with a learning procedure that does not require segmented training examples.
neurips-2007-learning-visual-attributes-.tldr: A probabilistic model learns visual attributes from weakly supervised, unsegmented images and can locate those attributes in new images.

paragraphs: Loopy belief propagation has worked well empirically in many applications, but its behavior often lacks theoretical guarantees. This paper examines the max-product version for weighted matching on general graphs. The question is when the message-passing procedure converges to the correct solution and when it fails to converge.

The authors connect that behavior to a linear-programming relaxation of the matching problem. When the relaxation is tight, max-product converges to the correct answer. When the relaxation is loose, it does not converge. This gives an exact characterization for the studied setting by tying the algorithm's behavior to a property of a related optimization problem.

The connection matters because it turns a question about iterative messages into a question about the relaxation's relationship to the original matching task. The paper also applies max-product to self-organization in sensor networks, demonstrating its effectiveness for practical distributed matching. The theoretical result concerns weighted matching on general graphs; the application shows how the message-passing approach can support computation distributed across a network.
neurips-2007-linear-programming-analysis.tldr: For the studied weighted-matching setting, max-product converges correctly when the LP relaxation is tight and fails to converge when it is loose.

paragraphs: Recognizing many object categories in complex scenes requires deciding both what objects are present and where they are located. This paper approaches that task by comparing an input image with a large collection of labeled training images. The comparison uses an image representation chosen to support matching between scenes.

The approach relies on regularities across similar scenes: retrieved images can suggest plausible object identities and locations in the new image. A probabilistic model then transfers labels from the retrieved set to the input. Retrieval therefore supplies candidate explanations, while the probabilistic transfer stage turns those examples into recognition and localization predictions.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness on held-out test sets from the LabelMe database and examine the contributions of individual algorithm components. These evaluations support scene alignment as a practical route toward recognizing many categories. The core idea is to make previously labeled scenes useful as structured evidence: their object arrangements provide information that can be transferred when the system encounters a similar new scene.
neurips-2007-object-recognition-by-scene.tldr: Matching a new image to labeled scenes and probabilistically transferring their labels supports recognition and localization across many object categories.

paragraphs: Support vector machine training can become expensive in both memory and computation as the training set grows. This paper introduces a parallel training algorithm, PSVM, designed to distribute that work across multiple computers. Its design combines a smaller approximate matrix representation with selective loading of the data each machine needs.

The algorithm performs a row-based approximate matrix factorization. If n is the number of training examples, p is the reduced matrix dimension, and m is the number of machines, the stated memory requirement changes from O(n²) to O(np/m). The reported computation-time complexity is O(np²/m), with p assumed to be substantially smaller than n.

These expressions show how the reduced representation and distributed computation jointly shape the resource requirements. The factorization reduces the size of the mathematical objects involved, while parallel processing divides the work and storage among machines. Empirical studies using as many as 500 computers demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The findings support the proposed combination as a practical response to SVM scalability problems.
neurips-2007-parallelizing-support-vecto.tldr: PSVM combines approximate matrix factorization with distributed computation to reduce SVM memory requirements and training cost.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for reconstructing brain states from functional neuroimaging measurements, with an emphasis on responses to naturalistic stimuli. It extends multivariate regression from discretized fMRI observations to stochastic functional measurements. This allows the analysis to work with voxel timecourses as functional data within the regression model.

The method searches for spatially distributed sets of voxel timecourses that optimize a multivariate functional linear model according to an R-squared criterion. Population-based incremental learning carries out that search. Voxel-wise nonlinear registration aligns stimuli with the fMRI data while accounting for variation in haemodynamic delay across brain regions and across people.

The aim is to capture distributed patterns that predict the stimulus, without trying to assign a function to a single localized brain area. Applied to previously unknown fMRI data, the method identifies distributed clusters that are highly predictive of particular stimuli. The result supports combining functional regression, spatial search, and timing alignment to recover predictive information spread across multiple brain locations.
neurips-2007-predicting-brain-states-fro.tldr: Functional regression with voxel-wise timing alignment identifies distributed fMRI patterns that predict naturalistic stimuli in unseen data.

paragraphs: The learning task is to predict nearly as well as the best function in a finite reference collection. Performance is measured by generalization error, with the goal of making the additional error as small as possible. The paper examines whether a favorable average guarantee for progressive mixture rules also implies favorable behavior across individual training samples.

Under suitable assumptions on the loss, the known expected-error guarantee has an additional term proportional to log|G|/n, where G is the reference set and n is the training-set size. These assumptions typically hold for squared loss with bounded outputs. The expectation averages over the random training set, which is central to understanding what this guarantee says.

The authors show that, for appropriate reference sets, the deviation convergence rate can be no better than order 1/√n rather than the anticipated 1/n. Thus, fast improvement in expected error can coexist with substantially weaker deviation behavior. The paper also supplies an algorithm that avoids this drawback, addressing the distinction between average performance and control of departures from that average.
neurips-2007-progressive-mixture-rules-a.tldr: Progressive mixture rules can achieve fast expected-error rates while having slower deviation rates; the paper provides an algorithm that avoids this drawback.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning builds a decision rule from both labeled and unlabeled examples. Boosting methods have been adapted to this setting, but the authors identify a missing ingredient in existing approaches: local smoothness constraints during ensemble learning. Such constraints express a preference for the decision rule to behave smoothly among nearby data.

The paper introduces a local smoothness regularizer within an optimization framework based on margin cost functionals. This places the smoothness preference directly into the boosting objective. The regularizer is designed to apply to existing semi-supervised boosting algorithms, providing a common way to incorporate this information during the construction of the ensemble.

The stated benefits are improved generalization and faster training. Comparisons on synthetic data, benchmark tasks, and real-world tasks demonstrate the regularizer's effectiveness. These results support using local relationships among examples as part of semi-supervised ensemble learning. The contribution is an adaptable regularization mechanism and empirical evidence for its value across the evaluated settings, together with a discussion of its relationship to previous work.
neurips-2007-regularized-boost-for-semi-.tldr: A local smoothness regularizer can improve generalization and accelerate training in existing semi-supervised boosting algorithms.

paragraphs: When observations are expensive, a system must choose which ones to obtain before making a decision. This paper considers a robust version of that problem: the chosen observations should perform well even when an adversary selects the evaluation objective. Applications include Gaussian-process regression, experimental design, and sensor placement for detecting outbreaks.

The proposed Submodular Saturation algorithm applies when the candidate objective functions satisfy submodularity, a diminishing-returns property. Under this condition, the authors establish strong approximation guarantees. They also prove a matching computational barrier in the stated sense: better approximation algorithms would require efficient algorithms for NP-complete problems.

Real-world evaluations complement the theory. For Gaussian-process regression, the method compares favorably with geostatistical heuristics while being simpler, faster, and theoretically supported. For robust experimental design, it performs favorably against methods based on semidefinite programming. The contribution combines practical observation selection with guarantees tied specifically to submodular objectives, making the structure of those objectives essential to the theoretical result.
neurips-2007-selecting-observations-agai.tldr: Submodular Saturation selects observations robustly against adversarial objectives, with strong approximation guarantees when those objectives are submodular.

paragraphs: Latent Dirichlet allocation groups co-occurring words into topics, but applying it to images requires deciding what visual words and documents should be. Its bag-of-words assumption makes spatial structure difficult to represent. This paper introduces Spatial Latent Dirichlet Allocation to incorporate the relationships among nearby visual observations.

The key change is in document construction. Spatial information enters through the assignment of visual words to documents, rather than through the values of the words themselves. Those assignments become hidden random variables instead of a partition fixed in advance. A generative procedure allows spatial knowledge to enter as a prior favoring nearby words being grouped together.

This makes the grouping of image evidence part of inference and gives spatial proximity a direct role in defining the model's documents. The authors apply the method to discovering objects in an image collection and report better performance than ordinary LDA. The finding supports the usefulness of learning spatially informed document assignments for the evaluated object-discovery task.
neurips-2007-spatial-latent-dirichlet-al.tldr: Spatial LDA learns how visual words form documents using spatial priors, improving object discovery over ordinary LDA in the reported evaluation.
